video_title: Making data centers flexible so they can serve the grid rather than stress it out
gist: Emerald AI's founder explains how its Emerald Conductor software makes AI data centers curtailable — via temporal (down-clocking/deferring jobs), spatial (geo-shifting workloads at fiber speed), and resource (on-site batteries/gensets) flexibility — so operators can buy faster, larger grid interconnections instead of waiting a decade in queue. He argues flexible load is worth ~100 GW of headroom on the existing US grid, displaces new gas build, cuts capex on both batteries and grid upgrades, and must become legally enforceable (ERCOT-style controllable load resource) rather than a 'regulatory fiction' as PJM's market monitor calls it.

themes.theme: Flexibility mechanics and the orchestration stack

insights.claim: Data center load flexibility decomposes into three complementary levers — temporal (down-clocking GPUs, pausing/checkpointing, reallocating GPUs across jobs), spatial (moving AI jobs hundreds or thousands of miles at fiber speed within latency bounds), and resource (on-site batteries and generators reducing net grid withdrawal) — and the commercial value comes from orchestrating all three together, not choosing one.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: The addressable stack spans IT scheduling software, on-site storage/UPS/gensets, and utility dispatch — vendors positioned in only one layer are substitutes for a component, not the system.

insights.claim: The orchestration platform is not confined to compute — it reaches into on-site batteries, microgrids, UPS systems and backup generation, executed via partnerships with Siemens, Eaton and GE Vernova, with the software acting as the 'brain' above the incumbent hardware controls.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Industrial electrical OEMs are being pulled into the AI-power control layer as partners and investors; watch their data-center segment commentary for this software-plus-hardware attach.

insights.claim: The platform's architecture deliberately abstracts away heterogeneous GPU hardware and telemetry so that, from a grid operator's viewpoint, a data center presents itself as a battery or controllable generator — making it schedulable inside existing dispatch systems.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: If large loads can be modeled as dispatchable resources, ISOs can count them in capacity planning — a structural change to how peak-driven transmission and generation capex is justified.
insights.quote: that data center presents itself to you as if it were a battery or a controllable generator

insights.claim: Workload flexibility tiers are supplied by the AI customer as job tags (priority 0–100 plus attributes like preemptability, throttle-ability, checkpointability, residency), not inferred by the software — meaning the flexibility resource is only as deep as customers are willing to declare.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: The realistic curtailable fraction is a customer-behavior variable, not a technical constant — a key uncertainty when underwriting flexibility-based interconnection deals.

insights.claim: Different job types have different physical limits: benchmarking runs cannot be down-clocked without corrupting results, fine-tuning runs can be both deferred and down-clocked, and latency-bound serving inference must be geo-shifted rather than slowed.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Flexibility depth varies by data center's workload mix — training/fine-tuning-heavy sites are more valuable flexibility assets than pure low-latency inference sites.

themes.theme: Business model and where the money actually is

insights.claim: The counterparties paying for load-flexibility software span the whole value chain — electric utilities, data center operators, leading AI companies buying compute, and cloud providers — rather than a single buyer.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Multi-sided revenue reduces single-customer concentration risk but means pricing power sits with whoever most needs the interconnection — currently the compute buyer.
insights.quote: it is electric utilities, data center operators, leading AI companies that are using compute, cloud companies

insights.claim: The dominant value proposition is interconnection speed and size, not energy savings: an existing site can go from 50 MW to 75 MW immediately instead of waiting ~10 years, and a new build can skip a queue described as 12 years, because the utility avoids building grid infrastructure to serve it.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Flexibility is priced against the option value of years-earlier GPU revenue — an enormous willingness-to-pay that dwarfs demand-response economics and could reprice interconnection queue position.

insights.claim: Demand response and flexibility-market payments are explicitly acknowledged as 'far less lucrative' than interconnection access, so an already-connected, non-expanding data center has weak incentive to adopt flexibility today.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: The retrofit TAM for existing sites is thin until either DR compensation rises or flexibility becomes a condition of service — near-term growth is tied to new-build and expansion pipelines.

insights.claim: Power cost optimization is currently not top of mind for AI buyers — the only question is getting GPUs energized at any cost — but as inference scales, power becomes the dominant variable cost of inference and cost pressure will make flexibility economically attractive on its own.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: A shift from land-grab to unit-economics discipline in AI compute would open a second, price-driven demand channel for power-optimization software.
insights.quote: Today, the key driver of value in the minds of data centers and clouds and AI companies is can I get the GPUs connected to power at any cost?

insights.claim: Failure liability is allocated contractually rather than technically: utilities can impose financial penalties or physically flip the breaker on non-compliant loads, while the software vendor's role is to guarantee the customer's protected workloads are not degraded.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Breaker-control and three-strikes clauses in interconnection agreements are the enforcement mechanism to watch — they determine whether flexible-load capacity is bankable.

themes.theme: Scaling from demos to commercial megawatts

insights.claim: The company has completed five demonstrations globally — including a sub-megawatt Nvidia GB300 test in Hillsboro, Oregon with Portland General Electric and a London demo with Nvidia — and says it has now exited the demo phase into commercial multi-megawatt whole-data-center deployment.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: The commercialization milestone is the gating fact for whether utilities can begin counting flexible load in planning — verify with PGE and EPRI DC Flex disclosures.

insights.claim: A 96 MW test facility with Nvidia and Digital Realty is slated to come online later this year and would be the first ~100 MW-scale power-flexible data center — a two-order-of-magnitude jump from the sub-megawatt demos.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated proof point: success validates flexible-load capacity credit at utility-relevant scale; failure resets the timeline for the entire thesis.
insights.quote: the 96 megawatt Verubin test center with Nvidia and digital realy comes online

insights.claim: In the first commercial multi-megawatt curtailment event the data center's power briefly breached the utility's curtailment limit before being corrected — an honest admission that control precision is not yet perfect at scale.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Overshoot risk is exactly what market monitors will cite against counting flexible load as firm capacity; watch published performance metrics from commercial events.
insights.quote: the data center power briefly breached or went right back above the limit of the curtailment that the utility had asked

insights.claim: Real-world failure modes are mundane infrastructure problems, not AI problems: GPU nodes go down or fail to report (often installation or power-equipment issues rather than chip issues), and in one demo power telemetry arrived only every 15 minutes instead of every second, forcing the control system to operate with Mars-like latency.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Sub-minute metering and telemetry inside data halls is an unglamorous but necessary hardware upgrade cycle if flexible load is to scale.
insights.quote: only happened every 15 minutes

insights.claim: The company has demonstrated a 24-hour continuous curtailment event to prove a facility could ride through a substation outage and repair — a duration no economically sized on-site battery could cover.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Long-duration curtailment capability is the differentiator versus storage — it lets utilities defer substation-level capex, not just shave peaks.
insights.quote: we actually just did a 24-hour event to prove that if the local substation went down and they had to repair for 24 hours, could you curtail?

insights.claim: The company deliberately open-sources its failure data and publishes peer-reviewed results and code (including with Nebius, Nvidia, National Grid in London, and EPRI, showing 200+ grid events met while protecting token throughput of critical workloads) as a regulatory trust-building strategy.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Publishing verifiable performance is how flexible load earns regulatory capacity credit — the moat is regulatory trust more than proprietary code.

themes.theme: Compute orchestration vs. batteries — the capex argument

insights.claim: Sizing on-site batteries to cover multi-hour or multi-day curtailment obligations is cost-prohibitive; the cheaper architecture is a short-duration (e.g. 2-hour) battery covering part of the load with computational orchestration carrying the rest and all longer events.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: If adopted, this caps the behind-the-meter BESS attach rate per data center rather than eliminating it — a moderating signal for storage demand forecasts tied to AI buildout.
insights.quote: Good luck trying to size the super expensive battery to provide all of this flexibility

insights.claim: Compute orchestration has near-zero marginal cost with event duration — hour three or hour twenty-four costs no more than hour one — whereas battery cost scales directly with duration, which is the core economic asymmetry favoring software flexibility.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Value concentrates in the tail of long, rare grid events — exactly the events that drive transmission and peaker capex today.

insights.claim: An investor-originated framing holds that data center interventions can be arranged on a merit-order dispatch curve like generation, and inherently flexible AI jobs (batch inference, fine-tuning) appear as very cheap, short vertical bars that should be dispatched *before* the on-site battery.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO), citing Kale Khan of Energy Impact Partners
insights.so_what: If compute curtailment sits below storage on the demand-side merit order, it structurally undercuts behind-the-meter storage utilization economics at AI sites.

insights.claim: The stated ambition is to move flexibility from rare emergency edge cases to routine daily operation — the company has already flexed a commercial site at the peak of the duck curve — which would make compute curtailment a normal grid balancing resource rather than a reliability backstop.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Routine flexing would compete with peakers and short-duration storage in daily net-load balancing, not just in scarcity hours.

themes.theme: Workload mix, geo-shifting and distributed data centers

insights.claim: Frontier training runs are counterintuitively the *least* amenable to load flexibility because they are massive, highly synchronized operations spanning many data centers — contradicting the common assumption that training is the easily deferrable workload.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: The largest and most publicized AI campuses may be the hardest to make flexible — flexibility capacity will come from fine-tuning, batch inference and mixed-workload fleets instead.
insights.quote: if you're training uh Opus 5 or GPT6, it's a massive, highly synchronized operation

insights.claim: The binary training-vs-inference framing is rejected as an oversimplification: fine-tuning of open-source models by enterprises is expected to become a large compute category, and latency-insensitive batch inference remains highly flexible even as inference share grows.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: The shift toward inference does not necessarily shrink the flexible load pool — a counter to the bear case on demand-response depth in AI data centers.

insights.claim: Live serving inference has been geographically shifted in production between Virginia and Chicago within chatbot latency bounds in work with Oracle — demonstrating that even latency-sensitive traffic is a spatial flexibility resource.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Cross-regional load shifting links regional power markets through fiber — a mechanism that could arbitrage price and congestion differences between PJM and MISO-style regions.
insights.quote: We've moved queries from Virginia to Chicago at the speed of light

insights.claim: A project with EPRI, Nvidia and Prologis aims to build multiple 5–20 MW data centers at individual distribution substations that are orchestrated together into a single 'virtual' aggregated data center exploiting whatever slack each substation has at a given moment.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: A distribution-level siting model would open industrial real estate portfolios and stranded distribution capacity as an alternative to gigawatt greenfield campuses.

insights.claim: Power flexibility is framed as a fundamental attribute of compute that extends beyond commercial grids — enabling AI to run on naval ships or forward-deployed theaters with imperfect power and fluctuating power envelopes.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: A defense/edge adjacency for compute-power orchestration software that is unpriced in the pure utility-market framing.

insights.claim: PJM's market monitor has labeled data center flexibility a 'regulatory fiction' because the RTO can request but not enforce it, and therefore will not plan around it — the central credibility obstacle to counting flexible load as capacity.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Until an RTO grants capacity credit to flexible load, the resource cannot displace generation or transmission capex in planning models — the key regulatory catalyst to watch.

insights.claim: The vendor explicitly supports making flexibility promises both legally and technically enforceable and concedes the market monitor is right that historical demand response performance has been poor — arguing AI data centers are a new class of controllable load rather than a repeat of legacy DR.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: An incumbent-technology skeptic's prior — that DR under-delivers — is the explicit bar this thesis must clear; performance data from commercial deployments is the falsifier.
insights.quote: And the market monitor is right to say, hey, historically, the performance just hasn't been great of demand response.

insights.claim: ERCOT's framework is cited as the model: a flexible data center connects as a 'provisional controllable load resource', is dispatched through the ISO's dispatch system, bids a willingness-to-curtail price (illustratively $2,000/MWh), and is legally equivalent to a generator or battery as a condition of interconnection.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Texas is the template other ISOs may copy; states adopting an ERCOT-style controllable-load tariff become the near-term markets for flexible data center capacity.
insights.quote: They say a flexible data center is welcome to connect. It'll be a what we call a provisional controllable load resource.

insights.claim: Mandating flexibility for all data centers is rejected in favor of a carrot approach — legacy heterogeneous cloud facilities are said to be poor flexibility candidates, and the incentive is simply that inflexible connections take far longer.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Bounds the retrofit market: the opportunity is new AI-purpose facilities, not the installed base of general-purpose colocation.
insights.quote: There are a lot of existing or legacy data centers that do a bunch of heterogeneous cloud computing tasks that probably aren't great candidates for flexibility

insights.claim: The forecast is that by 2030 gigawatt-scale data center load can no longer be added to the American grid without being flexible — flexibility becoming a standard condition of large-load interconnection within roughly five years.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: A dated, testable call: if right, flexibility capability becomes a required feature in data center design specs and a screening criterion for site valuations.
insights.quote: in the year 2030 you can add a gig gawatt of data center load to the American grid without it being flexible

themes.theme: Macro grid thesis: capacity headroom, gas vs. renewables, and rates

insights.claim: A 2025 Duke Nicholas Institute study (associated with Tyler Norris) found that if new loads curtail for just half a percent of their uptime, roughly 100 GW of new load could be added to the existing US grid without building new generating capacity — the analytical foundation the entire flexible-load industry is built on.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: If even partially realized, this headroom competes directly with the new gas turbine and transmission buildout currently being underwritten on AI load growth forecasts.
insights.quote: we can fit 100 gawatt of AI data centers onto the grid that we didn't think we could fit

insights.claim: The US grid is described as being used at roughly 50% of what it could deliver because generation, transmission and distribution are all sized for a handful of annual peak hours — meaning the binding constraint on AI load growth is peak coincidence, not total energy.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO), David Roberts
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI power shortage as a utilization problem solvable by software, which if believed reduces the urgency premium currently embedded in generation and turbine equipment demand.

insights.claim: The study's finding that 20% flexible demand avoids about a fifth of new gas construction (scaling roughly linearly to 50%) is endorsed as the founding motivation — flexible load is argued to pull intermittent renewables onto the grid by providing a responsive offtaker that consumes electrons when they are produced.
insights.speaker: David Roberts and Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: A direct bear case for the gas-turbine and gas-generation buildout tied to data centers, and a bull case for renewables + flexible offtake, contingent on flexibility scaling.
insights.quote: 20% flexible demand avoids a fifth of new gas construction

insights.claim: The near-term observable reality is acknowledged as the opposite of the thesis: hyperscalers are rushing to gas, the gas pipeline is jammed, gas company stocks are rising and on-site gas plants are being built — flexibility's renewables benefit is a future-state claim, not a current one.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: The host explicitly flags that current price action favors gas; the flexibility thesis is a timing bet on when demonstration converts into planning-model changes.

insights.claim: A recently published Nature paper concluding data centers are net bad for climate — largely because AI increases the efficacy of oil and gas extraction — is disputed on the grounds that it did not assume flexible data centers of the type being commercialized.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO), question from David Roberts
insights.so_what: The academic consensus on AI's climate impact currently runs against the flexible-load narrative — a headline risk for policy support and ESG-linked capital.
insights.quote: it's going to increase the efficacy of oil and gas extraction

insights.claim: The consumer-bill mechanism is spreading fixed network costs over more volume: if AI demand grows faster than new grid build, every megawatt-hour a flexible data center pays for helps amortize existing infrastructure, moderating rate pressure even if bills still rise for other reasons like fire hardening.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO), David Roberts
insights.so_what: The affordability argument is the political license for data center growth — utilities that can show flexible load moderating rates face less regulatory backlash on large-load tariffs.

insights.claim: Data centers going fully off-grid — or into space — is characterized as a death-spiral risk for utilities and an implicit cost increase because dedicated equipment cannot then serve the public grid, making grid-connected flexible load the preferred path.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames behind-the-meter islanded and orbital data centers as a competitive threat to regulated utility load growth — a scenario for utility revenue models.
insights.quote: You really don't want data centers to just entirely go off-rid or even worse go into space.

insights.claim: The long-run vision is a 'meta grid' where by roughly 2040 half the balancing work is done by the physical power grid and half by the AI/optical network shifting compute between nodes over fiber — with the speaker arguing AI could become 50% or more of American electricity demand and physical build simply cannot keep pace.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: If compute routing substitutes for transmission at scale, fiber and data center siting become partial substitutes for wires capex — a long-dated structural risk to transmission-heavy investment theses.
insights.quote: I see a future mid-century 2040 when half the work is done by the underlying physical power grid

insights.claim: Reframing data centers as energy technologies — controllable, dispatchable power users on par with nuclear plants or batteries — is presented as the core conceptual shift, with the aspiration that AI factories become the most exquisitely controllable energy asset ever on the grid because they alone can move load between locations at light speed.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: If regulators accept this classification, data centers gain access to resource-side market products and revenue streams historically reserved for generators and storage.
insights.quote: AI factory should be the most exquisitely controllable energy asset on the grid we've ever seen

insights.claim: The fusion of AI compute control and grid control is flagged by the operator itself as a security risk — two multi-trillion-dollar critical-infrastructure networks joined at a single software interface exposed to foreign and domestic intruders.
insights.speaker: Varun (Emerald AI founder & CEO)
insights.so_what: A new attack surface that could attract FERC/NERC-style cyber requirements, adding compliance cost and a moat for vendors that clear it first.

top_entities: Duke Nicholas Institute / Tyler Norris study
